sections.title: Fog: urgent work stays close
sections.intro: A machine cannot always wait for a remote cloud. Fog is a lightweight computing layer between end devices and the cloud.
paragraphs: A cloud-only factory sends machine data over a limited-bandwidth link to centralized storage and analytics. This is useful for large historical studies, but transmission and processing delay can be a problem for rapid process decisions. Fog nodes sit near a group of end devices, process some data locally, and send useful summaries upstream.

Prior filtration at the edge removes noise or unnecessary readings before they consume cloud bandwidth and storage. Fog can classify data, perform preliminary analytics, visualize a live process and support fast decisions; the cloud can train larger models, store history and coordinate many sites. Fog and cloud are complementary.

In this lecture’s simplified classification, the notes identify plant supervision and enterprise control as IT functions. Process control, sensor/actuator control, unit control and cell control belong to OT. A fog platform helps bridge both. The assignment key also lists merging real-time and non-real-time workloads as a fog-platform capability. Supervisory industrial functions can span IT and OT in practice; treat the lecture grouping as a teaching model rather than a strict universal boundary.
keyPoints: Three tiers: end devices → fog nodes → cloud; fog nodes may also communicate with one another.
Fog has less computation and storage than the cloud, but is closer to the data source.

sections.title: R: recognize the operators and workflow
sections.intro: R is an open-source language and environment for statistics, visualization and analytics; RStudio is an interface used to work with it.
paragraphs: Variables hold values: A = 20 is numeric, X = 'hello' is character, and Y = TRUE is logical. Reserved words such as if, else, repeat, while, function, for, next, break, TRUE and FALSE already have language meanings; they cannot be ordinary variable names. help(reserved) shows the reserved-word list.

Distinguish three visually similar operators. 1:5 creates the sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. 3 %in% c(1, 3, 5) checks membership and returns TRUE. 7 %/% 2 gives integer division, whereas 7 %% 2 gives the remainder. Powers use ^, comparisons use == or !=, and assignment commonly uses <-.

R objects package data differently. A vector is one-dimensional; a matrix has rows and columns; an array has multiple dimensions; a list can mix object types; a factor represents categories; and a data frame organizes columns into a table. The listed data types are logical, numeric, integer, complex, character and raw.

The lecture's iris demo installs caret and e1071 with install.packages(...), loads them with library(...), loads data(iris), and assigns dataset <- iris. trainControl(method='cv', number=10) selects ten-fold cross-validation; set.seed(...) makes random choices reproducible. An SVM is then trained and assessed using accuracy. Ten-fold means train on nine partitions and validate on the remaining partition, rotating through all ten.
keyPoints: Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, ^, %% (remainder), %/% (integer division).
Assignment: =, <-, ->; <<- searches outside the local scope and is not simply another spelling of local assignment.
Relational: <, >, ==, !=, >=, <=. Logical operations include & (elementwise AND), | (elementwise OR), and ! (NOT).
: creates a sequence; %in% checks whether a value belongs to a vector.
Matrix example: matrix(1:6, nrow=2, ncol=3, byrow=TRUE). Array example: array(1:18, dim=c(3,3,2)).
The assignment's validation method is ten-fold cross-validation, not a single train/test split.

sections.title: Julia: simple syntax, scientific computation
sections.intro: Julia is a high-level, open-source language designed for numerical work, with support for distributed computation and parallelism.
paragraphs: The lecture characterizes Julia as Python-like convenience with C-like performance. Treat this as a design motivation, not a guarantee that every Julia program is as fast as every C program. println(...) prints a value; typeof(...) reports its type. sections.title: Data management: clean before you analyze
sections.intro: Managing data means controlling its whole lifecycle, including storage, archiving, security, disposal and the policies that govern it.
paragraphs: Industrial data comes from enterprise trading, finance, sales and inventory records; machine sensors; biomedical measurements; and other large scientific sources. IIoT data can be large, fast and varied. Acquisition collects and logs readings, transmits them through networks, and preprocesses them before storage and analysis.

Preprocessing has three separate jobs. Integration combines sources into a unified view. Cleaning fixes or removes incomplete, inaccurate or incorrect records. Redundancy mitigation detects repeated data and uses filtering or compression to avoid wasting network and storage capacity.

Storage may use NoSQL databases or distributed file systems. The notes list key-value, column-oriented and document-oriented NoSQL families, plus GFS, HDFS and KosmosFS as file-system examples. SQL/relational and NoSQL systems can both be appropriate; the lecture highlights NoSQL for large and varied data rather than proving that all IIoT data must use it.

Analysis can involve Bloom filters, parallel computing, hashing, indexing, clustering, classification, neural networks or SVM. Automated industrial data management makes raw-material consumption, energy use, plant utilization and diagnostics available across the value chain. Availability matters because unavailable measurements cannot guide decisions.
keyPoints: Process order: generation → acquisition → storage → analysis.
Sensory data includes sound, vibration, chemicals, pressure and temperature; mobile data includes location, barcodes, images and video.
Inter-DCN transmission is between data centres; intra-DCN transmission is within one.
Integration combines; cleaning corrects; redundancy mitigation removes repetition.
Cloud traits recalled here: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

sections.title: Hadoop: storage, processing and resource allocation
sections.intro: Hadoop is an Apache framework for distributed storage and processing of large datasets across clusters.
paragraphs: Give each module one job. Hadoop Common supplies shared utilities. HDFS stores data reliably across DataNodes, using replicated blocks for fault tolerance. MapReduce divides a processing job into work that can run across machines. YARN, Yet Another Resource Negotiator, allocates and manages cluster resources for applications.

In HDFS the NameNode is the metadata authority: it tracks files, blocks and the DataNodes that hold them. DataNodes hold actual blocks, report block information to the NameNode and verify checksums. A user reading a file needs the metadata to locate blocks, but the NameNode is not the main store for every file's content.

The source describes JobTracker on the master and TaskTrackers on worker nodes. These are Hadoop 1 / MapReduce v1 terms. Keep them as historical lecture facts; modern YARN separates resource management into ResourceManager and NodeManager roles. Do not treat JobTracker as an intrinsic current HDFS NameNode duty.

MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database used with Hadoop for complex analytics. The course lists batch aggregation, data warehousing and ETL. MongoDB supplies a data-management view; Hadoop contributes distributed analytical processing. The assignment selects batch aggregation as one application.
keyPoints: YARN is the keyed answer for assigning CPU, memory and storage/resources; HDFS's primary role is storage.
MapReduce processes large data in parallel; Common supports the other modules.
NameNode = metadata; DataNodes = replicated file blocks.
Block replication supports tolerance of a node failure; it is not proof that every possible failure is harmless.

sections.title: Data-centre networks: connect the computing fleet
sections.intro: A data centre houses many servers, storage devices and network links. Its network must move traffic reliably within and between facilities.
paragraphs: In the three-tier design, edge or Top-of-Rack switches connect servers in a rack. Aggregation switches collect rack traffic. Core switches connect the aggregation layer and external networks. The notes give 1 or 10 Gb/s at the edge and around 10 Gb/s at higher tiers as course-era examples.

Good DCNs are stable, secure, reliable, scalable and agile. Agility means any service can run on any server at any time. Desired capabilities include VM migration while retaining an IP address, multiple usable paths, failure detection and efficient repair, and self-healing management.

A conventional three-tier tree can struggle with scalability, failure tolerance, energy efficiency and cross-sectional bandwidth. Fat-tree creates multiple paths using structured pods. For a k-ary fat-tree, each pod has (k/2)^2 servers, k/2 edge switches and k/2 aggregation switches; there are (k/2)^2 core switches. With k=4, that means four servers per pod, two edge and two aggregation switches per pod, and four core switches.

DCell is recursively constructed and uses server connections plus small switches to reduce single-point dependence. BCube is a server-centric modular-data-centre topology with multiple short parallel paths; its named source-routing protocol is BSR, BCube Source Routing. No topology eliminates every real-world failure.

IIoT can create many small sensor messages, increasing aggregate inbound bandwidth despite each message being small. Security, privacy, storage, high availability and changing bandwidth requirements matter. A Software-Defined Data Centre virtualizes network, storage and servers to provide programmable infrastructure and workload management.

sections.title: SDN: separate deciding from forwarding
sections.intro: Software-Defined Networking separates the control plane, which decides forwarding rules, from the data plane, which applies them.
paragraphs: In a traditional network, each forwarding device carries substantial local control logic. SDN exposes rule-controlled forwarding and gives applications a logically centralized controller view. Logical centralization can be implemented with multiple physical controllers for scale and fault tolerance.

The data layer contains routers/switches that forward packets. The control layer contains the controller and network operating system. The application layer contains business logic. Southbound APIs connect control to data; northbound APIs connect control to applications. OpenFlow is the named southbound protocol in the course.

Flow rules match packet fields and specify actions. Fast rule storage, often TCAM, has limited capacity. If another rule is needed, a system might replace an existing rule or combine rules using a wildcard. For example, multiple addresses may be covered by a less-specific prefix; combination must preserve the intended policy.

SDN design considers rule placement, controller placement and security. Controllers need resilient placement and secure links to forwarding devices; DoS and unauthorized rule changes remain risks. Applications include traffic engineering, load balancing, dynamic access control, mobility management and backbone network management.
keyPoints: Data plane forwards; control plane decides; application layer expresses business needs.
Southbound: controller ↔ devices. Northbound: applications ↔ controller.

sections.title: Software-defined IIoT and automation
sections.intro: Apply programmable networking and virtualization to industrial control, while respecting deadlines, availability and security.
paragraphs: Software-defined IIoT connects machine sensors/actuators at the device layer to a control layer and then to cloud business applications such as billing, analytics and security. The interfaces repeat the SDN pattern: southbound toward devices and northbound toward applications.

Network segmentation separates traffic groups with different policies. Policy-based forwarding changes priorities as process needs change: temperature alarms may matter more than humidity updates during overheating. Remote control can activate or adjust devices, but requires identity, authorization and secure command paths.

Required properties include low-latency virtualization, deterministic or predictable networking, high availability, fault tolerance, robust security and cost-effective application updates. Priority rules help express needs; they do not by themselves prove a hard real-time guarantee.

The course's automation hierarchy places sensors at level 0, digital controllers at level 1, supervisory systems such as SCADA/PLC/HMI at level 2, and business logic/analytics at level 3. Software-defined automation virtualizes control and supervisory functions and links software services to physical devices through the DCN. Sensors and actuators remain physical even when their interfaces or representations are virtualized.

Main SD-IIoT challenges: segmentation, policy forwarding, remote control and security.

sections.title: SDN across sensors, edge, grid and buses
sections.intro: The same control pattern repeats: monitor the network, provide a data service, then manage and optimize it.
paragraphs: A software-defined sensor network monitors sensors, acquires data and manages/optimizes operations. A public network monitors links and provides transmission services. Industrial cloud control monitors process units and provides processing; industrial bus control monitors bus states and provides processing services. In each case, applications sit above control and physical forwarding or sensing sits below.

TSCH means Time Slotted Channel Hopping. Devices communicate in scheduled slots and change radio channels to help deal with interference. 6TiSCH brings IPv6/6LoWPAN into TSCH-based constrained networks. Software-defined 6TiSCH must handle lossy links and the extra control traffic generated by a controller.

The lecture's slicing mechanism allocates communication resources between end devices and control functions, providing dedicated forwarding paths while reducing control overhead. The assignment specifically places slicing at Layer 2. The stack highlighted in the notes is IEEE 802.15.4 → TSCH MAC → 6LoWPAN header compression. uSDN is a lightweight stack described as running on Contiki.

Software-defined edge architecture includes industrial devices, access devices or cluster heads, edge/fog nodes, a controller and industrial cloud. The assignment calls its streams ordinary and emergent. Fog nodes and access devices serve delay-constrained emergent services, so an urgent event can receive nearby processing rather than await a remote service.

The smart-grid control layer includes a centralized controller with DMS, DERMS and SCADA functions, plus interface management, maintenance, fault discovery, security and topology management. OpenFlow can be costly for constrained devices, motivating lightweight and fog-enabled designs rather than simply imposing a data-centre stack on every sensor.

sections.title: The Mininet demo: rules make SDN scalable
sections.intro: An emulator can create a small virtual network on one computer so forwarding policies can be observed.
paragraphs: Mininet emulates the network; Open vSwitch supplies OpenFlow-enabled virtual switches; POX is the SDN controller; D-ITG generates traffic; and the application chooses Shortest Path Delay (SPD) routes. The demo uses a Barabási–Albert topology and UDP traffic.

Packets without a matching rule may cause a packet-in event to the controller. The controller selects behavior and installs a rule. Subsequent matching packets are forwarded at the switch, so the controller does not need to process every packet in the flow.

The reported experiment had 24 flows and 74,150 packets. The controller received only 277 packet-ins, of which 202 were UDP. Reported outcomes were about 218 ms average delay, 18 ms jitter, 4,578 kbps throughput, 1.85% drop and zero QoS-violated flows under that experiment's conditions.

The source's environment used POX on port 6633, OpenFlow 1.1, Python 2.7 and NetworkX on a Google Cloud machine with about two vCPUs, 7.5 GB RAM and 50 GB storage. The listed minimum environment was two CPU cores, 4 GB RAM and 20 GB storage. These are historical demo details from the cited 2018 setup, not a requirement to install obsolete software.

sections.title: Security goals, trustworthiness and risk
sections.intro: IIoT protection must account for information and physical consequences together.
paragraphs: Industrial devices often have limited energy, processing, buffer space and bandwidth. Many vendors, protocols and legacy systems create heterogeneity. Connecting more devices enlarges the attack surface. The consequences can include stolen data, stopped production, machine malfunction, accidents and harm to people.

CIA stands for confidentiality, integrity and availability. Confidentiality limits who can read useful data; integrity guards against unauthorized alteration; availability keeps authorized access and services usable. These goals overlap with, but do not exhaust, system trustworthiness.

The five trustworthiness properties in the lecture are security, privacy, reliability, resilience and safety. Reliability means operating correctly for a specified time under stated conditions. Resilience means continuing to function correctly under dynamic adversarial conditions; safety concerns avoiding unacceptable physical harm.

IT emphasizes information protection, privacy and reliable services. OT emphasizes safe physical operation, resilience and reliability. IIoT convergence requires a shared trust model, including third-party cloud services and incoming commands. Physical isolation and old IT assumptions are insufficient as the only protections.

The risk treatments listed are avoid, mitigate, outsource/transfer, accept and balance residual risk. Threat actors may be external criminals, unethical insiders, outsourced providers, hardware vendors or service suppliers. A trusted contractual role does not remove the need for access controls, updates and risk evaluation.

sections.title: STRIDE, attack layers and responsibility
sections.intro: Use a threat vocabulary to ask what can go wrong, then identify who must build and maintain the protection.
paragraphs: STRIDE names six categories: Spoofing identity, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege. A person pretending to be an operator is spoofing; altering a setpoint is tampering; denying a performed action is repudiation; leaking a recipe is information disclosure; exhausting a service is DoS; gaining extra rights is elevation of privilege.

The lecture groups attack surfaces into application, network and physical levels. SQL injection abuses application queries, replay resends an old message, man-in-the-middle intercepts or modifies communication, sniffing observes packets, misrouting sends traffic incorrectly, and jamming disrupts radio communication. Device tampering attacks the physical equipment.

Trust responsibilities propagate through the lifecycle. The system owner defines operational requirements, evaluates risks and ensures timely patches. The system builder designs a cost-efficient trustworthy system, defines component trust requirements, and tests/certifies the system. Component builders deliver hardware, software and services that meet those requirements.

Coordination matters: organizations should identify threats early, adapt security measures and respond quickly. Hardware modules, interfaces, virtual machines and IaaS/PaaS/SaaS services all contribute to system trust; checking one component once is not enough to cover its entire lifecycle.

Tampering attacks integrity; information disclosure attacks confidentiality; DoS attacks availability.

sections.title: Protect the devices, links and all data states
sections.intro: End-to-end protection must cover where data is born, where it travels, where it is stored and where it is used.
paragraphs: The five protection areas are end devices, fog devices, cloud, communication and data, coordinated by security management. Horizontal protection concerns peer devices at the same layer. Vertical protection concerns interactions between layers or parts of the stack. Industry-specific requirements add to shared IIoT needs.

End-device controls include physical protection, verified identity, appropriate access rights and data protection. Authentication checks who a device/user is; authorization checks what it may do. The keyed choice for resource-constrained devices is lightweight symmetric-key cryptography, supported by energy-efficient authentication and intrusion detection/prevention. Lightweight must still mean appropriately secure.

Fog nodes are more capable than end devices but remain semi-constrained; protect fog identity and fog-to-cloud access. Cloud protection covers data, applications, infrastructure, provider-access policies, identity management and physical security. A third-party provider adds trust and responsibility questions rather than removing them.

Data at rest is stored, data in transit is moving, and data in use is actively processed. Apply confidentiality, integrity and availability to each state. Protect not only sensor readings but commands, actuation signals, logs and security-configuration messages. Firewalls, gateways, access controls and suitable cryptographic mechanisms protect communications.

Security management handles configuration, patches and controls, with prevention, detection, analysis and mitigation. Its monitoring cycle combines monitoring, response and analysis. The healthcare example includes embedded devices, fog and cloud, with device authentication, protected communications, access-controlled cloud data and SDN-based monitoring.

The course names ISO/IEC 15408 (Common Criteria) for IT security evaluation, IEC 62443 for industrial automation/control security, and NIST SP 800-82 for industrial-control/OT guidance. The assignment specifically selects NIST SP 800-82. The source's claim that no IT/OT-convergence standard exists is historical lecture context, not a verified present-day standards survey.

sections.title: Smart factories: four levels, five traits
sections.intro: Connected production links workers and machines to plant execution and enterprise planning.
paragraphs: Traditional factories may have isolated machines, unbalanced workloads, limited live data and long changeovers. A smart factory connects the process so machine health, quality and production status can guide decisions. It aims to reduce changeover and production time, improve maintenance and support new products or components.

The four levels are field devices, shop floor, plant and enterprise. Field devices include sensor-enabled tools and worker wearables. Shop-floor controllers use suitable networks such as ZigBee or Bluetooth in the examples. At plant level, MES coordinates execution and control rooms. Enterprise ERP and cloud services consolidate planning, storage, analytics and visualization.

The five traits are connected, optimized, transparent, proactive and agile/flexible. Connected means exchanging data; transparent means making the state visible; proactive means anticipating problems; optimized means improving operations; flexible means adapting process parameters and configuration. The assignment's question about optimally adjusting machine configuration, material flow or temperature selects flexibility.

The company examples are lecture-era case studies. Airbus uses connected manufacturing, robots, AR/computer vision and predictive analytics. KUKA links robots to a private cloud; DeWalt tracks construction workers/equipment through IoT and Wi-Fi mesh; ABB YuMi supports human–robot collaboration. Amazon's robotic shelves have a reported 20% operating-cost reduction in the 2014 example.

Other examples: Caterpillar uses AR and predictive maintenance; Fanuc's Zero Downtime uses sensors/cloud analytics; Gehring connects honing machines; Maersk monitors shipping assets, fuel and refrigerated containers; Magna Steyr uses wearables, driverless transport and a digital factory. Rio Tinto uses autonomous trucks/trains/drilling; Bosch improves working conditions and reduces errors.

Hitachi's Lumada layers in the notes are Edge, Core, Analytics, Studio and Foundry; Transport is not a layer. North Star BlueScope Steel uses smart helmets/wristbands to monitor worker health and detect radiation and toxic gases. These names are quiz cues, not claims about every current product configuration.

sections.title: Food IIoT: trace a product from field to consumer
sections.intro: The same sensing, networking and analytics tools can improve farming, processing, logistics and food transparency.
paragraphs: The field-to-plate chain begins with sowing and growing, followed by harvesting, processing, packaging, transport, wholesale, retail and consumption. Networked sensors can measure environmental and product conditions; communication links stakeholders; applications serve farmers, retailers, government, consumers and insurers.

End-to-end traceability links a finished item to its source and journey. A packet of rice could be traced back to the paddy field when records are complete. Benefits include efficient production, food safety/compliance, supply-chain transparency and lower waste. Traceability records the journey; condition monitoring checks whether the journey preserved quality.

Farm uses include weather, crop maturity, insect, soil-moisture, water-level, fertilizer and nutrient sensing. Livestock systems monitor health, feeding and barn/hatchery temperature. GPS can track animals/equipment; drones monitor fields; predictive maintenance monitors tractors. Factory connections help quality, time to market, compliance and worker safety.

The course's SmartLabel example uses a QR code to provide ingredients, allergens, nutrition, certification, handling and related product information. Intellicup has an NFC chip at its base, paired with e-wallet/QR functions and an IntelliHead dispensing unit to reduce waiting. BioRanger detects food pathogens with a handheld device and Android app.

Other named examples are CityCrop's indoor climate-controlled growing, Eskesso app-controlled Wi-Fi cooking, a Culinary Science Flavor Matrix using data/ML for pairings, Spinn smart coffee brewing and Farmshelf indoor farming. Treat product names/features as course examples rather than current purchase recommendations.

sections.title: Healthcare: measurements become useful knowledge
sections.intro: Networked medical and wearable devices support remote monitoring and communication between patients and care teams.
paragraphs: Patient sensors can observe blood pressure, respiration, pulse, heart rate, weight, glucose or temperature. Gateways send readings to an IoT cloud service that verifies, processes, analyzes and stores them for authorized healthcare applications. The course's five-stage sequence is sensing, sending, processing, storing and learning.

Telecare and telemedicine can reduce travel and support monitoring at home. Hospital examples include smart-bed activity notifications, hygiene monitoring and emergency-unit planning. Sensors and alerts support professionals; these educational examples do not establish that every device can diagnose a condition or replace clinical assessment.

Device associations to learn are QardioCore for ECG, Dexcom for continuous glucose, iHealth BP5 for blood pressure and Kinsa for temperature. Pulse oximetry concerns oxygen saturation. The source also describes IoT contact-lens glucose monitoring as a technology example. ADAMM, an asthma-monitoring example, uses body temperature, cough rate and heart rate to identify early warning patterns.

Mobile examples include Health Assistant, Google Fit for physical activity and ECG Self Monitoring / ECG Self Check. Challenges include limited compute, memory and energy, patient mobility, growing device diversity and scalable algorithms without compromised security. Protect confidentiality, integrity, authentication and availability.

The notes motivate healthcare IoT using ageing-population figures: approximately 382 million people aged 60+ in 1980 and a projection of 2.1 billion in 2050. These are the lecture's historical figures/projection, not newly verified population statistics.

sections.title: Power plants: from monitoring to autonomy
sections.intro: Smart grids carry information as well as electricity, allowing demand, equipment and faults to be managed more actively.
paragraphs: A traditional grid mainly delivers energy to a passive consumer. IIoT adds measurements and information exchange across generation, transmission, distribution and consumption. Consumers and distributed resources can participate through demand scheduling, customized service and electric-vehicle integration.

The course's maturity sequence is monitoring, control, optimization and autonomy. Monitoring uses connected sensors. Control adds actuators and feedback. Optimization analyzes accumulated data to improve performance. Autonomy extends decision-making to device, system and application levels. The stage immediately after optimization is autonomy.

The three-layer architecture is sensing/perception, gateways/network, and applications. Sensors, RFID, cameras and audio devices sit at sensing; enterprise/access/home gateways connect through wireless, mobile or satellite networks; applications include smart homes, offices, EVs and transmission services. Fog is close to sensing while cloud supports higher-level services.

Network names describe scope. HAN connects home devices using examples such as ZigBee and 6LoWPAN. NAN covers neighborhood/distribution aggregation. FAN connects distribution controllers, regulators and data collectors; the key lists WiMAX, 3G and 4G wireless and Ethernet wired. WAN connects wider areas. These are course-listed choices, not an exhaustive current network catalogue.

Benefits include remote turbine/transformer monitoring, fault detection, demand scheduling, self-healing, blackout prevention, voltage stabilization and better energy efficiency. Other examples are water pressure/quality and leak prediction, wind-turbine control, solar fault monitoring, smart pumps/boilers, SCADA plants and digital twins.

Challenges include security/privacy, resource constraints, scalability, unpredictable delay and inconsistent protocols/security design. The notes' approximately 200 ms or more cloud round-trip delay is an example-dependent value, not a universal cloud latency. Time-critical control needs timing analysis and appropriate local control.

The Meter Data Acquisition System, MDAS, gathers meter readings. The Meter Data Management System, MDMS, manages and analyzes the collected data. The quiz asks which component analyzes data, so choose MDMS rather than MDAS.

Smart energy meters support electricity networks; smart water meters support water systems. Analytics can reveal unusual use, losses or trends, while access controls and data protection are needed because usage patterns can be sensitive. The source's widespread-deployment remarks describe lecture context.

sections.title: Inventory and quality: know what you have
sections.intro: Inventory is a usable but idle resource with economic value. Management balances availability against the cost of holding it.
paragraphs: A bakery needs enough flour to meet demand but not so much that money is tied up or materials spoil. Inventory management controls ordering, storing and stock movement. It meets anticipated demand, smooths production and distribution, protects against stock-outs, supports order cycles and can respond to price changes or quantity discounts.

The supply chain described is raw materials → suppliers → manufacturers → distributors → warehouses → retail shops → customers. Sensors and RFID provide identification, location, condition and stock movement. Networks connect purchasing, materials, production and sales, while analytics supports demand forecasts and replenishment.

Effective management tracks inventory, forecasts demand, handles lead time and its variability, estimates holding/ordering/shortage costs, and classifies stock. Lead time is the gap between placing an order and receiving it. The more variable that gap is, the harder it is to prevent shortages using a simple fixed schedule.

Quality control routinely checks product/service standards, ensures correct and complete data, fixes errors and omissions, and documents/archives inspections and inventory activity. Condition sensors and analytics complement identification: knowing where a food lot is does not alone establish that it stayed within temperature requirements.

Comprehensive visibility in the assignment means inventory levels, expiration dates, item locations and forecast demand. RFID can also support shelf identification, storage-temperature monitoring, damage assessment, shrinkage/shortage/overstock detection and route planning. Adoption challenges include scattered/inconsistent data, human error, training expense, security gaps, hidden costs and potential disruption during rollout.

sections.title: RFID: battery presence does not tell the whole story
sections.intro: An RFID system uses a tag, a reader and backend information systems; tags communicate through radio.
paragraphs: A passive tag has no internal power source and draws energy from the reader field. It responds by backscattering rather than running its own active transmitter. The course describes passive tags as comparatively small, thin and inexpensive.

An active tag has its own power supply and active radio transmission, offering longer-range behavior and additional capabilities at greater cost/size. The assignment divides active tags into transponders and beacons. A transponder-style response is triggered by an interrogation; a beacon periodically broadcasts.

A semi-passive or battery-assisted passive tag has an onboard battery for its IC or sensing functions, but no active transmitter in the course taxonomy. It still communicates through backscatter. That is the key distinction from the active-tag answer.

Compared with a conventional barcode workflow, RFID can be read without optical line of sight and can identify multiple tags in a suitably designed read zone. Tags can link identities to additional records or store additional data. These benefits depend on reader design and environment; RFID is not automatically secure, and barcodes can also link to rich backend information.

sections.title: Plant safety: protect people, equipment and commands
sections.intro: A connected plant adds network/software protection to the physical protection of workers and machinery.
paragraphs: Worker wearables can measure physiological and ergonomic conditions; machine/truck sensors reveal operating state. Collected data supports monitoring and approved feedback commands. The intrusion triangle lists motive, means and opportunity. Security controls aim to reduce the opportunity or means rather than assuming every possible attacker lacks a motive.

OT protection covers devices and machines; IT protection covers networks and software. The notes' software goals are authentication, integrity and availability. For the assignment, availability is functioning time divided by total time: if a service works for 990 of 1,000 observed hours, its observed availability is 0.99 or 99%.

Network segmentation divides a network into smaller parts and explicitly applies policies to each. Supporting controls include privilege-based access, firewalls, VPNs, IDS/IPS, endpoint/mobile protection, anti-malware, behavioral analytics, data-loss prevention, email/phishing controls, cloud security and SIEM. Segmentation can limit propagation but must be engineered and enforced.

The assignment's mobile-security answer is a secure web gateway, described as detecting attacks early and using cloud-integrated security to help stop spread between branches. This is a key/architecture-specific capability, not a guarantee that every gateway identifies every future attack.

AR glasses can overlay leak warnings and safe-exit guidance onto the real scene. VR presents a simulated environment, useful for training examples. Both depend on software and trustworthy content: corrupted instructions or displays can create physical risk, so these systems need integrity and access protection as well as useful sensors.

sections.title: Facility management: maintain the place, people and process
sections.intro: Facility management guides operations and maintenance for property owners, covering infrastructure as well as finance, people and contracts.
paragraphs: A manufacturing facility can include buildings, machinery, trucks and fleet infrastructure. Stakeholders include owners, customers, tenants, contractors and subcontractors. Facility management integrates people, place and process, alongside support functions such as finance, IT, HR and administration.

A single-facility system collects IoT measurements into a common database and monitoring station. A multi-facility system combines multiple collection units and sites at a manager/control station, sometimes involving subcontractors. Keep security and privacy boundaries explicit across those relationships.

The important record covers every asset, machine, fault, repair, usage pattern and modification. Analytics can use this history to predict needs, prevent hazards, ensure consistent decisions and optimize manpower, technology, assets and cost.

Applications include smart lighting, refrigeration, meters, fire suppression, safety/security alarms, HVAC, room reservation and stocks/supplies. Real-time room status can prevent double booking; occupancy/space analytics can estimate office square-foot utilization. The exact-utilization phrase is the assignment's named analytics application.

IoT addresses the cost barrier by increasing operating efficiency and reducing maintenance cost. Other benefits include energy management, remote monitoring, better customer experience, intrusion tracking and productivity. Challenges include balancing quality with budget, aging assets, regulatory change and security. These are possible outcomes from a well-run implementation, not automatic savings from attaching sensors.
